title: How many passengers fly from or to Heathrow on an average day? A worked market sizing answer
description: A step-by-step estimate for "How many passengers fly from or to Heathrow on an average day?" with the approach, the maths and a sanity check.
hook: Here is a harder one to practise on. Read the question, pause, and have a go at your own estimate first, even a rough one. Then walk through the answer below and compare. Your number does not need to match; your logic is what counts.
body:
The question

How many passengers fly from or to Heathrow on an average day?

The approach

Supply side: flights per day × seats per flight × share of seats filled.

Say this out loud before you touch any numbers. It lets the interviewer agree with your plan, or nudge you, before you have done any work.

Step by step

  1. Take-offs and landings per day: 1,300
  2. × 180 seats per flight
  3. × 80% seats filled

That gives about 187k passengers a day.

Does it make sense?

Long-haul jets carry far more than 180 people, so the true figure is likely higher. Say so as a caveat.

This sanity check is the step most people skip, and one of the easiest ways to impress. It shows you care whether the number is right, not just whether the sum works.

Real-world check

Heathrow handled about 84.5 million passengers in 2025, roughly 230,000 a day, from around 478,000 take-offs and landings (about 1,300 a day). So the flight count in the estimate is right, and the gap is seats per flight: long-haul jets carry far more than 180 people.

Source: Heathrow media centre: record year 2025.

Your turn

Try a similar question in the free market sizing drill, which checks your logic step by step.
outro: If your estimate was far off, look for which step made the difference. That is where the learning is, and it is exactly what an interviewer would ask about.
